title: The Real US Energy Security Problem—And How to Fix It - Taylor & Francis
description:
1 “Statistical Review of World Energy,” 2025, Energy Institute, 2025, 21, https://www.energyinst.org/statistical-review/.
32 Statistical Review of World Energy 2025, Energy Institute; Jeff D. Colgan, “Fueling the Fire: Pathways from Oil to War,” International Security 38, no.
48 Statistical Review of World Energy 2025, Energy Institute.
55 Statistical Review of World Energy 2025, Energy Institute.
57 US Department of Energy, “History of SPR Releases,” accessed November 7, 2025, https://www.energy.gov/ceser/history-spr-releases.
text:
The United States has an oil security problem. The economic damage of a global oil shock would disproportionately harm the United States compared to its peers including China, Russia, and the European Union. That may seem surprising. The United States became a net exporter in 2020, currently leads the world in oil production, and its 2024 output of 20 million barrels per day (mb/d) was the highest ever recorded by a single country.Footnote1 But production and export levels do not drive economic vulnerability to oil shocks. Oil trades in a global market at one global market price. Sudden price spikes affect everyone consuming oil across the global market, regardless of individual countries’ output levels.

The United States is disproportionately susceptible to price spikes because US gross domestic product (GDP) relies more heavily on oil consumption, dollar per dollar, than peer economies. What determines a country’s vulnerability to price shocks is the oil intensity of its economy, i.e., how much oil consumption is required to generate each unit of GDP. The more heavily a country’s economic output depends on oil, the greater the damage it is likely to suffer from sudden oil price increases.Footnote2 Unfortunately, the oil intensity of the US economy is among the highest in the world and eclipses that of any other major power, even China—which is surprising, because in many ways China is still a developing country, and developing countries tend to be less oil efficient than fully industrialized countries. Because US economic output relies more heavily on oil consumption than any of its peers or rivals, it is likely that oil price spikes would disproportionately damage its economy. Thus, the oil security problem confronting the United States is not “just” a prosperity issue, but a matter of relative economic gains (and losses) in the event of an oil shock, with ramifications for the balance of power.

The nature of US oil vulnerability remains poorly understood, even by policy experts and the informed public, as myths and misconceptions have clouded energy issues for decades.Footnote3 It has been apparent to Washington since the early 1970s that the United States faces an oil security problem, however murky the official understanding of it may be, and that the political volatility of the Middle East, the world’s most important oil producing region, raises the potential for supply disruptions. The flexibility of oil markets can cushion the impact of disruptions more than policymakers realize, but the United States and other countries use policy tools to provide additional insurance beyond market adaptation. Unfortunately, policymakers’ misunderstandings of the oil market have led the United States to adopt policies that are ineffective, costly, or misguided.

Misunderstandings of the oil market have led the US to adopt ineffective, costly, or misguided policies

The core of the US energy security strategy is to keep large contingents of troops in the Middle East to prevent disruptions to oil supply. But this has proven an enormously expensive endeavor based on an exaggerated idea of military threats to oil supply. It also does nothing to prevent price shocks from outside the Middle East, such as the 2022 shock accompanying Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. So, the costs of this strategy badly outweigh the benefits. Another common recommendation said to produce greater energy security—increasing domestic oil production—misunderstands the problem. Whatever the merits of increased domestic production, energy security is not among them. Because oil is a global commodity, meaning it has one price, domestic producers would be part of any price shock, not an antidote to it.

The United States could simply worry less about oil price shocks, exit the Middle East, and rely on the strategic petroleum reserve as well as market adjustment to reduce the economic impacts of a disruption. But if policymakers really want to heighten energy security, their best bet is to electrify the US vehicle fleet. Switching the transportation sector from oil-burning cars to electric vehicles (EVs) would dramatically decrease the oil intensity of the US economy and reduce US vulnerability to price shocks. This would be a far cheaper and more effective route to increase energy security than keeping large garrisons of US forces in the Middle East.

The national security benefits of EVs are a major reason why the Chinese government has pushed them aggressively.Footnote4 For years, Washington worried that Beijing would build up its military forces in the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean to protect maritime oil supply routes from US naval interdiction.Footnote5 Instead, China is ridding itself of oil dependence altogether, and with it, its reliance on the Middle East. Thanks to significant investment in EVs and high-speed electric trains, Chinese gasoline consumption peaked in 2023.Footnote6 Total Chinese petroleum consumption is expected to fall at least 27 percent by 2050, and could decrease by as much as 52 percent by that year if government goals are met.Footnote7 Those projections could very well be underestimates because China has beaten expectations about EV adoption before. Simply put, China is solving its “Malacca Dilemma”—its reliance on the Strait of Malacca for oil imports—with EVs. The United States should too.

US Economic Dependence on Oil

Oil supply shocks are linked to economic recessions, which is why the United States and other countries seek to avoid them.Footnote8 US households cannot quickly decrease oil consumption when prices are high, so they instead cut back expenditures on other goods and services, depressing economic activity.Footnote9 The reason US consumers cannot cut production in response to high prices is because oil is singularly important to the present-day US transit system, which relies on internal combustion engines (ICEs). While substitutes to oil exist for many purposes—generating electricity and heat, for example—nothing can adequately substitute for oil in powering ICE vehicles because oil is the most energy-dense fuel on the planet, containing more energy per unit of volume than any other combustible fuel.Footnote10

US transportation depends almost completely on petroleum, with oil and oil products supplying 88 percent of the energy used for transit in the United States. This is down over the last twenty-five years, with oil providing 97 percent of total transportation energy in the year 2000. (The decrease was equally driven by the mixing of biofuels like ethanol into gasoline and the uptake of natural gas-powered vehicles in mass transit systems.)Footnote11 The transportation sector accounts for 68 percent of US oil demand, while the industrial sector is a distant second at 27 percent of demand.Footnote12

Contrary to popular assumptions, very little oil is used in the United States to generate electricity, which consumes less than half of 1 percent of demand.Footnote13 Less than 1 percent of electricity produced in the United States depends on oil, which means that electricity prices in the United States are immune from global fluctuations in oil prices.Footnote14 Instead, electricity relies on a diverse mix of primary energy sources that are produced domestically including natural gas (37 percent), nuclear (25 percent), coal (24 percent), and renewables (12 percent).

US economic reliance on oil far surpasses that of its peers, which means that a spike in oil prices would disproportionately harm the United States. Per capita oil consumption in the United States dwarfs that of similar countries, with the average American consuming twenty barrels of oil annually in 2023, compared to nine barrels for the average Russian, seven barrels per EU citizen, and four barrels per person in China.Footnote15 The oil intensity of the US economy, which measures how much petroleum is needed to produce each unit of GDP, is unusually high. In 2023, the Russian economy was roughly 20 percent less oil intensive than the US economy, China’s economy was 30 percent less oil intensive, and the EU was almost 50 percent less reliant on oil than the United States.Footnote16

A spike in oil prices would disproportionately harm the United States

All major economies are less vulnerable to oil shocks than in past decades. Global oil intensity has declined more than 50 percent since its 1973 peak, thanks to three main factors: technological improvements in energy efficiency; globalization, which allowed for the rapid diffusion of more energy-efficient technologies; and sectoral shifts in the global economy away from heavy industry, which tends to be very energy intensive, toward service sectors.Footnote17 Even a shock similar in scale to the 1970s oil crises could have a much-reduced impact today.Footnote18 But the relative consequences of a shock would be significantly worse for the United States.

Market Resilience and the Global Oil “Bathtub”

Middle East oil matters to all countries that consume petroleum, regardless of whether or not they import oil from the region, because oil trades in a global market at one global market price. Two factors underlie this point. First, petroleum is fungible, meaning that oils from different sources are substitutable for one another.Footnote19 Second, the cost of transporting oil is a tiny fraction of its overall price, meaning that market actors can easily switch buyers or sellers, even at great distance, without significantly affecting prices.

Experts often analogize the global oil market to a giant bathtub with many spigots and many drains.Footnote20 Each spigot represents a country that produces commercial quantities of petroleum, some fifty countries in 2024. The drains symbolize every oil-consuming country in the world. Oil enters the bathtub from every spigot and exits though every drain. It does not matter which oil molecules from which spigots end up in which drains. What matters is supply and demand and the size of the bathtub, i.e., the total amount of oil in the market. If global output increases, the tub level rises, and the global price of oil falls for everyone. If global production decreases, the tub level falls, and all consumers pay the higher global price.

The bathtub metaphor illustrates why targeted oil supply cutoffs are nearly impossible to implement. Producers cannot punish specific consumers by refusing to sell them oil because other global suppliers will simply step in to fulfill demand. The only way for a producer to increase prices is to withhold oil from the bathtub, which would reduce the global supply and raise prices for everyone, diluting the price increase across the whole market. The country harmed most would be the producer itself because it would lose oil revenue.

The global oil market is more resilient and adaptive to disruptions than policymakers realize, and reasonable people could argue that the United States does not need additional insurance to guard against disruptions. One study of all major supply shocks between 1978-2010 found that the market compensated adequately for price spikes, prevented any real physical shortages from emerging, and returned prices to pre-disruption levels within weeks or months.Footnote21 Even the 1973 oil embargo and production cuts orchestrated by the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries (OAPEC) were much less damaging than commonly assumed. Long lines and shortages in the United States resulted from poorly-designed price ceilings and rationing policies that interfered with the market’s ability to adjust.Footnote22 More recently, the 2019 drone attack on Saudi oil facilities in Abqaiq knocked 5.7 mb/d of production offline—volumetrically the largest oil disruption ever—and caused an immediate 15 percent price spike, but Saudi oil facilities were quickly repaired, no oil shortages resulted, and prices returned to pre-attack levels within two weeks.Footnote23

The global nature of the oil market is both a blessing and a curse for oil security. On the positive side, it provides significant supply security by buffering individual states from targeted disruptions and spreading out the pain of disruptions across all consumers. Oil can be rerouted from one source to another, or turned around and resold, assuming oil levels in the bathtub remain constant. The negative is that disruptions anywhere in the market can be felt by consumers everywhere, even in countries potentially capable of self-sufficiency like the contemporary United States.

Why the Middle East Matters

The Middle East has held towering importance to the global oil industry since large-scale production commenced after World War II, but few policymakers understand why. The Middle East does not, and never has, produced the majority of global supplies, and its oil volumes alone, while significant, are not what make the region special. By far, the largest cumulative producer of global oil has been the United States, which accounts for about 18 percent of all oil produced since the beginning of the commercial oil industry in 1859 (Russia accounts for 13 percent of cumulative global oil production and Saudi Arabia about 11 percent).Footnote24 Total Middle East production did not exceed US production until 1966, while Saudi Arabia, famous for its outsize role in the oil market, only outproduced the United States during a twenty-five-year stretch between 1992-2017.

What actually makes the Middle East important is its extremely low petroleum production costs, consistently the lowest in the world. Middle East oil is conventional oil, meaning that it naturally occurs as a liquid and can be extracted from the ground without advanced recovery techniques like horizontal drilling and fracking. It is also located close to the surface, making it especially cheap and easy to extract compared to other sources of conventional oil.

Middle East cost advantages are significant both for corporate breakeven prices, which determine the viability of new wells, as well as daily operating costs. According to estimates, the average 2025 breakeven price for new US oil production is about $62-64 per barrel, whereas the breakeven price for new Middle East production is just $27/barrel. Daily operating costs in the United States hover around $50/barrel, while Middle East operating costs are as low as $3-5/barrel.Footnote25

The major cost advantage for Middle East production means that the region will always contain the last producers standing that can competitively produce oil even throughout periods of sustained low oil prices, when higher-cost producers such as the United States, which relies heavily on enhanced recovery measures, would be pushed out of the market. It also means that Middle East proven oil reserves are the most robust in the world to price fluctuations. (Proven oil reserves estimate how much oil would be economically viable to produce given technology and expected market prices. As such, they are an economic measure, not a strictly geological one.) Reserves expand significantly when prices are high—as even high-cost production becomes competitive—and contract when prices are low. The low cost of Middle East oil means it is viable to produce even if future global oil prices are expected to plummet.

Strategies for Oil Security

The United States has adopted several policies designed to lessen its vulnerability to oil price shocks since the 1970s. The three most important have been 1) a robust US military presence to deter and defend against threats to Persian Gulf oil; 2) efforts to encourage domestic oil production (aka “drill, baby, drill”); and 3) the establishment of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) to ease market adjustments to supply disruptions.

The first two policies—US military presence in the Persian Gulf and “drill, baby, drill”—are deeply flawed. The United States should immediately stop costly and risky deployments to the Middle East because the region is not the only source of price shocks, and besides, no country can significantly threaten Persian Gulf oil access. “Drill, baby, drill” does not solve the vulnerability problem because global price shocks will affect US consumers no matter how much oil is produced domestically. The SPR does help to stabilize oil markets, as designed, and could be increased in size. Fortunately, the Trump administration is taking positive steps in this direction by replenishing some of the stocks removed from the SPR during the Biden administration, but those efforts should proceed more aggressively.

A fourth potential strategy, the electrification of the US automobile fleet, holds the best promise for reducing US vulnerability to price shocks and should be adopted to provide better insurance against disruptions.

The US should immediately stop costly and risky military deployments to the Middle East

Military Presence

Military presence has tried to prevent oil price shocks from occurring by using US military force to deter and, if necessary, defend against major military threats to Persian Gulf oil. It has been the primary US approach to ensure its oil security since the late 1970s, when the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, combined with the upheaval of the Iranian Revolution, raised fears that the Soviets might attack Iran next or threaten the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried two-thirds of global oil exports at the time.Footnote26

The possibility of Soviet domination over Persian Gulf oil during the Cold War was uniquely threatening because the USSR might have denied oil to the West in coordination with an attack on Western Europe, thereby hamstringing NATO’s ability to defend itself.Footnote27 President Jimmy Carter responded by pledging to use US military power to defend the free flow of Persian Gulf oil, a declaration that became known as the Carter Doctrine.Footnote28 To back up Carter’s promise, the United States developed a Rapid Deployment Force to deter the Soviets, which evolved into CENTCOM in 1983.

The purpose of the US military commitment was not to forestall minor oil disruptions but rather to prevent any single power from consolidating control over Persian Gulf oil. Accordingly, the United States avoided local conflicts which had no realistic chance of creating a regional hegemon that could engineer major supply disruptions. For example, US forces refrained from intervening in the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War until 1987, despite years of Iraqi attacks on Gulf oil tankers. (Those attacks were ineffective, and, after an initial spike, oil prices actually decreased throughout the war.)Footnote29 It was superpower rivalry that finally drove the United States to reflag Kuwaiti tankers in 1987—after the Soviets offered to do so first.Footnote30

The end of the Cold War removed the Soviet menace to Gulf oil, but Saddam Hussein’s annexation of Kuwait in August 1990 and aggressive moves toward Saudi Arabia heralded a new regional hegemonic threat that warranted US military intervention.Footnote31 If Saddam conquered Saudi Arabia as well as Kuwait, the combined resources of all three countries would give him control over 15 percent of global production and 46 percent of known oil reserves—perhaps enough to unilaterally dominate global markets.Footnote32

The United States responded by deploying over 500,000 troops to defend Saudi Arabia under Operation Desert Shield, which George H.W. Bush explicitly justified on the grounds of protecting free access to Persian Gulf oil.Footnote33 After Saddam failed to comply with UN Security Council Resolution 678, which called on Iraq to withdraw from Kuwait by January 15, 1991, the United States led an international coalition in Operation Desert Storm to liberate Kuwait. From the defeat of Saddam until the 2003 US invasion, the United States maintained a standing military presence in neighboring countries to contain Iraq and enforce no-fly zones in the north and south to protect Iraqi civilians from Saddam’s repression.

Oil, per se, was not the reason why the United States deposed Saddam in 2003, though it remains murky whether the stated rationale of preventing Saddam from acquiring weapons of mass destruction was the true motive or merely pretext.Footnote34 But the fact that Iraq is located in a crucial oil-producing region was the primary reason why Washington viewed an aggressive, potentially nuclear-armed Saddam as dangerous. It is nearly impossible to imagine the United States worrying so much about Saddam’s aggression if the targets of his expansionism had no oil.

Policy Shortfalls of Military Presence Today

The most glaring problem with the military strategy is that it only buys insurance for price shocks originating in the Persian Gulf. But price spikes from outside the Gulf region are no less potentially damaging. Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine caused a 50 percent increase in global crude oil prices due to market speculation and boycotts on purchasing Russian oil.Footnote35 As a result, US gasoline prices topped $5 per gallon in June 2022, the highest level ever recorded.Footnote36 The presence of US troops in the Middle East obviously did nothing to ameliorate that shock, whereas investment in EVs—being demand rather than supply focused—would ease the consequences of price shocks from any source by reducing total US reliance on oil.

The military strategy does nothing against price shocks outside the Gulf region like Russia

Even within the Middle East, the military approach has been unnecessary, costly, and ultimately ineffective. The toppling of Saddam in 2003 removed the only plausible hegemonic threat to the region’s oil, with the three major Persian Gulf powers—Iran, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia —unable to conquer one another, and China posing no military threat now or in the foreseeable future.Footnote37 Fears that Iran could close the Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20 mb/d of global oil flows, are so exaggerated that one analyst has dubbed the waterway the “Strait of Hyperbole.”Footnote38 Current global oil inventories are 7.9 billion barrels, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA)—enough to compensate for a complete closure of Hormuz (an event unlikely in the extreme) for 395 days.Footnote39

Nevertheless, massive US forces have become a Middle East fixture, numbering some 40,000 US troops at present.Footnote40 Simply maintaining the US military footprint in the region has been estimated to cost between $6.75 billion to $101 billion (2025 dollars) per year, not counting the cost of military operations.Footnote41 US presence has also generated costly political backlash. Continued US deployments in Saudi Arabia following the Persian Gulf War helped to inspire Osama bin Laden to form al-Qaeda and perpetrate 9/11 and other terrorist attacks.Footnote42 Were it not for oil, a major US troop presence in Saudi Arabia would have been unlikely, and without that presence, bin Laden would not have targeted the United States so ardently, if at all. The extensive costs of the post-9/11 Global War on Terrorism against al-Qaeda, including the twenty-year US war in Afghanistan, are therefore indirectly attributable to the 1990s US mission to protect Saudi Arabian oil.

Keeping US troops in theater unnecessarily exposes them to risks, as demonstrated when Iran attacked the al-Udeid Air Base in Qatar in summer 2025 in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities.Footnote43 US presence also risks further entangling the United States in regional conflicts despite widespread agreement that Washington must rebalance its commitments away from the Middle East. If oil mattered less to the US economy, there would be even less reason for Persian Gulf deployments and the United States could bring more troops home.

“Drill, Baby, Drill”: Maximizing Domestic Oil Production

The strategy currently being pushed by the Trump administration is to increase US domestic oil production in hopes of attaining “energy security” and reducing US economic vulnerability to hostile foreign actors.Footnote44 Yet, whatever merits “drill, baby, drill” might have, it will not solve the problem of price spikes due to the global nature of the oil market. Trump has taken many steps to encourage greater US petroleum output. Among his first actions in office was to sign an executive order declaring a national energy emergency and another executive order to loosen federal regulations in order to fast-track fossil fuels development.Footnote45 Trump’s signature legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill passed by Congress in July 2025, further incentivized domestic production by opening up new lease sales on federal lands, loosening rules for pipeline permits, and limiting environmental reviews.Footnote46

“Drill, baby, drill” will not solve the problem of price spikes due to the global nature of the oil market

The domestic production approach has historical antecedents in President Richard M. Nixon’s response to the 1973 oil crisis. Shortly after Arab states announced the oil embargo and production cuts, Nixon launched his “Project Independence” initiative in November 1973 to boost US output by deregulating oil markets and loosening environmental protections—for instance, by mandating approval of the Trans-Alaskan Pipeline, which had been bogged down with court challenges.Footnote47 Yet, despite Nixon’s policies—which were continued by Ford, Reagan, and others—US production declined for the next four decades, failing to surpass its 1973 output again until 2014, amidst the shale boom.Footnote48

Policy Shortfalls of “Drill, Baby, Drill” Today

Whether Trump’s initiative will create a lasting boost for US output remains unclear because the primary economic factor driving production is oil prices, and these have been relatively low since Trump began his second term. US oil output increased last year, but rig counts have steadily declined since January 2025, and several US oil companies have cut staff or announced plans to do so, signaling a possible slowdown ahead.Footnote49

Even if Trump’s efforts significantly increase US production, it will not solve the basic problem that US oil prices are beholden to global market forces and are affected by supply shocks around the world. As long as the United States is connected to global oil markets, it will remain vulnerable to price spikes, even if it could provide all its own oil domestically.

To truly be “oil independent,” the United States would have to close its markets to foreign oil and disconnect from the bathtub. Theoretically, the United States could do this, but it would be economically counterproductive. American consumers would lose the benefits of being able to buy cheaper foreign oil and would have to pay higher prices due to high US production costs. That would unnecessarily strain the US economy compared to the economies of countries paying the global price.

The United States would also lose flexibility to draw on global supplies in case of domestic disruptions. Petroleum imports (combined with releases from the US strategic petroleum reserve) significantly eased US oil prices after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita knocked out some 30 percent of US refinery capacity in fall 2005, for example.Footnote50 When a 2021 cyberattack shut down the Colonial Pipeline, a vital artery transporting oil from the Gulf of Mexico to the East Coast, petroleum imports from the global market rapidly compensated for stranded supplies, minimizing the price shock.Footnote51 As these examples show, staying connected to the bathtub offers significant diversification benefits even for self-sufficient countries.

The United States has experimented with detaching itself from global markets in the past and US consumers ended up paying much higher prices at the pump. In 1959, President Dwight D. Eisenhower restricted oil imports to prop up the high-cost US petroleum industry, which was at risk of being undercut by cheaper foreign oil. By 1970, oil import controls resulted in US customers paying $3.30 per barrel when world prices were just $2 a barrel—a price premium of 65 percent.Footnote52 At the time, US authorities justified the premium as necessary to preserve a strategic industry in the context of Cold War competition with the Soviets. It is difficult to imagine US consumers signing up for such a price differential now, particularly when the US pacing competitor—China—would continue paying world prices.

Strategic Petroleum Reserves

The current US policy tool that best addresses price shocks is the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which was written into law in December 1975 as another federal response to the 1973 energy crisis. The SPR is an emergency crude oil stockpile with a storage capacity of over 700 million barrels that can be tapped to calm oil markets in times of crisis or disruption.Footnote53 Its primary facilities are located in converted salt domes in coastal Texas and Louisiana, near major US pipelines and refineries. It takes about two weeks for SPR oil to hit the market, with an initial maximum drawdown rate of 4.4 mb/d that tapers off within weeks to months, depending on fill levels.Footnote54 That amount would cover over 20 percent of US oil demand and over 50 percent of gross US imports, which were 8.4 mb/d in 2024 (net US imports are negative because the United States exports more oil than it imports).Footnote55 The present inventory of the SPR is about 410 million barrels (as of October 31, 2025).Footnote56 The SPR uses two types of drawdowns to moderate oil prices: emergency drawdowns, which are large sales of oil usually conducted to support US foreign policy objectives; and exchange agreements, which loan SPR oil, usually in smaller quantities, to US companies to cushion non-strategic shocks such as those occurring from US pipeline problems, weather events, or the Covid pandemic.Footnote57

US presidents have broad authority to initiate large emergency drawdowns of the SPR and have done so on four occasions. Each release appeared to succeed in lowering oil prices, though how much of the price decreases should be attributed to the SPR, as opposed to overlapping situational factors, is impossible to know. President George H.W. Bush directed the first emergency release on January 16, 1991, mere hours after the United States launched Operation Desert Storm to push Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait. The commencement of Desert Storm had initially caused oil prices to spike by 25 percent from $32 to $40 per barrel, but by the next day, prices fell to just $21 per barrel.Footnote58 The SPR seems to have worked, but of course, other factors influenced prices downward, including the announced release of IEA oil stockpiles and the success of the US air war against Iraq, both of which likely reassured markets.Footnote59

Hurricane Katrina prompted the second emergency release of 11 million barrels of SPR oil in September 2005 alongside an exchange agreement loaning an additional 9.8 million barrels to US oil companies. SPR oil, in combination with a coordinated IEA release and increased imports of foreign oil, helped to ease oil prices after an initial shock.Footnote60

The third emergency petroleum drawdown occurred in June 2011 during the civil war and NATO bombing campaign against Colonel Muammar Qaddafi in Libya, which removed about 1.3 mb/d from the global market. In a coordinated response, IEA member countries released 60 million barrels of oil, 30 million of which came from the US SPR.Footnote61 Oil prices held steady at roughly $110 per barrel despite the SPR release, but a counterfactual analysis concluded that without the drawdown, prices would have spiked about 20 percent to $135 per barrel.Footnote62

The last and most recent emergency drawdown from the SPR occurred in 2022, when President Joe Biden authorized the sale of 180 million barrels over a ten-month span immediately following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in late February 2022.Footnote63 The invasion had caused global oil prices to spike 50 percent due to market speculation and sanctions on Russian oil.Footnote64 US Treasury Department analysis found that the SPR drawdown reduced US gasoline prices by about 40 cents per gallon.Footnote65

The four drawdown cases suggest that the SPR has been an effective tool for moderating the impact of supply disruptions. Critics, however, argue that the SPR is unnecessary because privately held industry stockpiles can suffice to cushion price shocks. Moreover, they caution that the SPR creates perverse incentives for private industry to maintain smaller inventories than they otherwise would, or to refrain from tapping their stockpiles in hopes that Uncle Sam would act first.Footnote66 Presidents may also misuse the SPR for political reasons, by releasing oil to lower prices and benefit the incumbent party before US elections.

The SPR has been an effective tool for moderating the impact of supply disruptions

These are valid criticisms. The particulars of when and how to employ the SPR are complicated and politically sensitive. But having an SPR—particularly when it is tapped in combination with private inventories and stockpiles held by IEA partner countries—is a far superior policy tool compared to “drill, baby, drill” or military presence in the Persian Gulf. Global oil stockpiles are mind-bogglingly massive and can make a major difference to markets. World inventories currently amount to 7.9 billion barrels according to the IEA.Footnote67

The gargantuan size of global inventories might make the US SPR seem unnecessary, even quaint. But still, it is wise for the United States to control some portion of global stockpiles to use as it sees fit, rather than be at the mercy of others. Moreover, by maintaining its own massive stockpile, the United States encourages its partner countries in the IEA to honor their stockpile commitments rather than free ride, which helps to keep global inventories so high.

Electrification

The best untapped means to insulate against oil supply shocks is electrifying the US automobile fleet by investing in EVs, mirroring the approach taken by China. Because transportation drives US demand for oil, electrification would dramatically decrease US petroleum consumption. In turn, that would reduce the oil intensity of the US economy and make it less vulnerable to supply shocks from the Middle East—or anywhere else.

The United States was on a decent track toward electrification before recent policy changes made by the Trump administration. Since January 2025, the Trump administration has ended subsidies for electric vehicles established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, rolled back investments in charging infrastructure, and weakened federal fuel economy rules by removing penalties for car companies that exceed corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) standards.Footnote68

As a result of these policies, economists have revised estimates of US electric vehicle adoption significantly downward, trailing both China and the rest of the world through at least 2040.Footnote69 Whereas by 2030, EVs were expected to make up 48 percent of new US car sales, projections now suggest they will comprise only 27 percent, compared to EVs representing 80 percent of new cars in China.Footnote70 There will be 14 million fewer EVs on US roads in 2030 than there would have been under previous policies.Footnote71

Chinese EV adoption continues to skyrocket even as uptake in the United States slows. The Chinese government has subsidized electric vehicle purchases since 2009 and the country has reduced its gasoline demand by over 1 million barrels per day thanks to substitution away from oil-powered cars.Footnote72 It is estimated that two-thirds of all electric vehicles sold worldwide in 2025 will be purchased in China, compared to just 7 percent of EVs being bought by US consumers.Footnote73 Within the next year, China’s EV sales will be larger than the entire US car market.Footnote74

China is also extending its dominance over EV manufacturing, accounting for 70 percent of total EV production in 2024.Footnote75 Recent breakthroughs in battery technology by two Chinese EV manufacturers, BYD and CATL, have enabled them to build rapid-charging EVs that can add hundreds of miles of range with a five-minute charge, putting them “pretty much a generation or two ahead of the rest of the world,” according to one expert.Footnote76

Had the United States kept its policies, it would have at least kept pace with China’s expected decreases in oil intensity, but progress is now in doubt. Assuming that pro-EV policies remained intact, the United States and China each would have reduced their oil intensity by about two-thirds by 2050. China’s economy would still be about 30 percent less oil intensive than the US economy, meaning China would remain significantly more resilient than the United States to price shocks, but at least the United States would have kept pace. Now, US vulnerability is poised to worsen relative to China’s.

The national security benefits of EVs are substantial, but that fact has been lost in the political crossfire over environmental policy. Rolling back incentives to electrify the fleet appears to be part of the Trump administration’s preference for encouraging US fossil fuels production rather than fostering the clean energy industry. Yet, electrification need not undermine US fossil fuels production because electricity generation does not need to be decarbonized to reduce US reliance on oil, and hence remove the need for US troops to stabilize the Middle East. The United States could plug its new EV fleet into coal- or natural gas-powered electric grids, or nuclear-powered grids for that matter, and still enjoy the full national security benefits of electrification.

Electrification of the fleet would be transformative for US energy security and finally release the United States from caring about far-off political events that could affect global oil prices. By getting off of petroleum, the transportation sector would switch from a fuel-intensive system, which is highly dependent on global oil prices, to a capital-intensive system, which would be much more insulated from the political risks associated with trade, despite its reliance on rare earths and critical minerals for capital construction.Footnote77

Electrification of the fleet would be transformative for US energy security

The mere mention of rare earth elements sends shivers down the spines of many in Washington who fear that the purported Chinese dominance over strategic minerals could be used to coerce the United States. Those fears are overblown.Footnote78 Moving to an EV-based transit system would actually reduce US vulnerability to trade chicanery, by China or anyone else, compared to the current oil-dependent system. While it is true that building new battery electric vehicles requires rare earth elements and other critical minerals that China has cost advantages in producing, once EVs are built, they no longer need such inputs to function. Thus, a disruption in strategic mineral trade, or an increase in mineral prices, would have no effect on consumers’ pocketbooks, unless they happened to be in the process of purchasing a new EV at the time.Footnote79 By contrast, because vehicles with internal combustion engines must constantly guzzle fuel, all drivers of traditional automobiles experience financial harm from supply shocks and price spikes.

The Way to US Energy Security Today

The global nature of the petroleum market means that if major supply disruptions occur anywhere in the world, the resulting global oil price increases will hurt US consumers, no matter where they get their oil. More concerning, the United States is disproportionately exposed to price shocks because the oil intensity of the US economy far exceeds that of its peers. Should a 1970s-style oil shock occur—or worse, a succession of shocks—US economic vitality would suffer relative to competitors like China and Russia. Economic strength is the basis of US military power. Therefore, a global shock that hurts the United States more than its rivals could contribute to shifting the long-run balance of power against the United States.

Major oil disruptions that overwhelm the capabilities of markets to adjust are unlikely, and one could reasonably argue that the United States does not need additional insurance against disruption risks. But given relative US vulnerability, the United States should at least make sure that the insurance it buys actually works. Fortunately, the policy answers are clear.

First, the US SPR works, and the government can take immediate steps to bolster its effectiveness even further. With oil prices relatively low and widespread expectations of a global oil glut ahead, the timing couldn’t be better for the United States to invest in replenishing the SPR to 700 million barrels or even upping it to 1 billion. That would require expanding the SPR storage capacity, which was estimated to cost about $3 billion in 2006, or roughly $5 billion today (adjusted for inflation).Footnote80 Fortunately, the Trump administration has pledged to refill the SPR, though its follow-through has been slow thus far.Footnote81 The United States could also encourage private companies to expand their inventories through tax breaks or other incentives. Internationally, the United States could negotiate with partner countries in the IEA to increase their stockpiles too and set rigorous guidelines for coordinated release to burden-share the costs of calming markets.

Currently, a global oil shock could shift the long-run balance of power against the US

Over the long term, the United States should resume investment in electric vehicles and nationwide charging infrastructure to speed the transition away from petroleum. Building out EV infrastructure can be compatible with a pro-nuclear and pro-fossil fuels outlook, as domestic coal and natural gas would be crucial for meeting increased electricity demand by EVs, as would nuclear energy. US oil production would continue for the export market, or perhaps someday could be used once again to generate US electricity. States that prefer clean energy could use their own policy levers to encourage solar and wind production—or not. The primary goal of EVs is to wean US transportation off of petroleum as quickly as possible to reduce disproportionate US economic exposure to the vagaries of the oil market. EVs don’t have to be green to dramatically transform US energy security. But US policymakers should not deceive themselves into thinking that increased fossils fuels production would enhance US energy security without parallel investments in EVs.

Most importantly, the United States should end its military commitment to protecting Persian Gulf oil and remove US troops from the region at long last. Staying offers little practical benefit for energy security but costs much—in terms of US soldiers killed or wounded, the ballooning of military budgets, and the risks of entanglement in a volatile region of diminishing strategic value. Resources saved from ending oil-related US military missions could be used to offset the costs of refilling the SPR and electrifying the US automobile fleet. With the EV transition afoot, when it comes to the Persian Gulf, the juice is no longer worth the squeeze—if it ever was.

text:
The administration is increasing the volumes of biofuels like ethanol that are required to be blended into other fuels for 2026 and 2027. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is finalizing what it described as “the highest levels in program history.”

The announcement came alongside other initiatives, like offering loan guarantees and easing pollution monitoring requirements that the administration says will help farmers.

The war has effectively closed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, raising the price of not only fuel, but also fertilizer.

President Trump also doubled down on his call for Congress to remove restrictions on selling high-ethanol gasoline in the summertime.

Some Corn Belt lawmakers sought to scrap those restrictions through a spending bill earlier this year, but lawmakers agreed instead to explore compromise legislation.

Trump said he was “trusting” Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) “to find a deal that works for farmers, consumers and refiners.”

Among the changes Trump announced Friday was easing EPA rules regarding pollution sensors for tractors and other equipment — a move the administration says will save the sector $14 billion.

title: Forever Chemical Regulation and Accountability Act Would Address PFAS in the Domestic ...
description:
On March 19, 2026, Representative Betty McCollum (D-MN) and Senator Dick Durbin (D-IL), Minority Whip, reintroduced the Forever Chemical Regulation and Accountability Act (H.R.
8016, S. 4153) to address the use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in the domestic supply chain.
According to McCollum’s March 19, 2026, press release, the bill would: Initiate a National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) study to review the persistence, bioaccumulation, and human health risks of PFAS.
NASEM would also identify current PFAS uses and provide guidance on classification of essential or non-essential uses that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) will use to require that uses designated “non-essential” be phased out; Require all PFAS manufacturers and users to file reports with EPA disclosing certain information relating to PFAS and require manufacturers and users to submit a phase-out schedule of their products to be completed within ten years; Direct EPA to facilitate phasing out non-essential PFAS production, consumption, and possession and prohibit manufacturers and commercial users from releasing any PFAS into the environment within ten years; Establish deadlines for manufacturers to remove PFAS from certain consumer goods, such as rugs, furniture, and child products; Reinforce that, to the maximum extent possible, PFAS should be eliminated from products or replaced by substitutes that reduce risk to human health and the environment.
McCollum and Durbin previously introduced companion versions of the bill in April 2024.

text:
When a 2023 Indiana law barred a state pension from investing with any fund manager that had made a commitment to environmental, social and governance goals, it marked a high point in the ESG backlash, which had sought to end corporate practices accounting for climate and other environmental impacts when making business decisions. The Indiana law targeted investment behemoths like BlackRock, which had earlier proclaimed its commitment to ESG in an annual shareholder letter.

As the media focused on the retreat from these once-popular funds, University of Virginia School of Law professor Quinn Curtis questioned if obituaries for ESG were premature. His investigation into the fund flows of ESG-branded investments culminated in his article “The ESG Backlash and the Demand for ESG Mutual Funds,” published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies in October 2025.

Curtis studied the data to figure out if there really had been declining interest in these funds in the wake of state laws and federal rules targeting ESG investing. His research led him to some surprising conclusions. Investor interest in ESG funds had already been waning before laws targeting ESG were enacted, but while demand has declined from its peak, ESG funds haven’t experienced significant outflows. Perhaps most significantly, both the rise and fall of interest in ESG was driven by traditionally dispassionate investors who were managing institutional portfolios, like pensions.

From Screening ‘Sin Stocks’ to Climate Activism

The term “ESG” may be a recent phenomenon, but investing for a social impact is not.

“Screening of ‘sin stocks’ has been around for a long time: weapons, tobacco, liquor, gambling,” Curtis told PLACE. Some investors would avoid or divest from these industries. In the 1990s, investors began making targeted investments to achieve social goals.

ESG fund managers instead began making commitments to “use the levers of corporate governance to change firms’ behavior,” Curtis said. One way to achieve this is voting to diversify a company’s board.

“ESG investing is really inseparable from concerns about climate change,” Curtis said. Investing in an ESG-branded fund often meant buying stock in companies committed to building the infrastructure for a clean energy transition.

A Growing Backlash

Curtis traced the early investor interest in ESG and the subsequent legal backlash in his paper. In the years before the pandemic, investors were willing to pay a premium for ESG-branded stocks, he explained. But this changed in 2020, save for a brief uptick in investor interest in 2021.

Crucially, Curtis argues that this declining interest pre-dated federal rules and state laws seeking to restrict ESG investing.

In 2020, the Trump administration enacted a rule requiring federally regulated retirement accounts to be invested to achieve pecuniary benefits. While an earlier version of the rule aggressively targeted ESG investing, the final rule largely preserved the status quo.

“The pitch for ESG was often that investing this way isn't just socially responsible; it's ultimately going to perform well in the long term,” Curtis said.

“If you want to make an argument that ESG investing is oriented towards pecuniary benefits, that’s open to you,” he explained. “You don't have a special burden under the rule, but they did make it clear that [ESG investments] had to be about risk and return.”

ESG-branded fund managers who had been investing for climate action argued that companies making money from the transition to zero-carbon energy would benefit both clients’ portfolios and the planet.

By 2020, the conservative American Legislative Exchange Council had circulated anti-ESG bills to state legislatures, according to Curtis’ paper. More than 20 states have now enacted these or similar bills, which use states’ limited power to curtail ESG investments by adding requirements to state pension fund investment strategies.

“I have my doubts that Texas or Florida, or many of these other red states ever had state pension assets invested in ESG assets,” Curtis said. Still, he looked at whether these state laws affected overall investor interest in ESG funds. Not only had excess demand for ESG-branded funds declined before these laws were on the books, but demand for these funds remained non-negative through 2024.

A Dent to the ESG Brand

Curtis said the biggest impact of the legislative backlash was likely on large investors like BlackRock that had publicly committed to ESG. He pointed to BlackRock’s website, which seems to have been scrubbed of ESG language.

“They definitely felt the heat, because they are among the asset managers who need to win these contracts [to manage state pensions], and they realized that being so far out front on the ESG issue was going to be a problem,” he said.

Pricing Climate Risk Remains Competitive

Although branding a product as an ESG fund may not spur investor interest as it once did, Curtis explained that climate risk remains an important pecuniary factor when pricing a company’s share. “ESG funds go from being the hottest section of the asset management industry to one more investment strategy that you can choose,” he said.

The bottom line is that while the ESG label might have faded, the metrics that ESG labeling sought to quantify remain.

“I think that there’s real money being spent to understand [climate] vulnerabilities and make sure that they're accounted for,” Curtis said. “But pricing those vulnerabilities accurately doesn't do anything to make climate change worse or better.”

name: North Carolina American Energy
title: Farm Waste to Energy Gains Ground Across the U.S.
description:
Farm-based biogas systems are gaining traction across the United States, reflecting a broader shift toward decentralized energy production.
While still a modest share of overall U.S. energy supply, the growth signals increasing confidence in the sector’s long-term role.
At the farm level, biogas systems are reframing waste management economics.
Methane capture helps address regulatory and sustainability pressures, while energy production creates an additional income stream tied to evolving energy markets.
Farm-based biogas could generate enough additional energy to power an estimated 7.7 million homes, positioning it as a practical contributor to both domestic energy supply and emissions reduction targets.
text:
Farm-based biogas systems are gaining traction across the United States, reflecting a broader shift toward decentralized energy production. Data from the American Biogas Council shows that 631 farms now operate these systems as of early 2026—more than double the total recorded in 2020.

Energy output has followed a similar trajectory. Annual production now exceeds 61 million MMBtu, up from approximately 23 million five years ago. While still a modest share of overall U.S. energy supply, the growth signals increasing confidence in the sector’s long-term role.

Investment activity underscores that momentum. In 2025, 41 new systems came online, representing roughly $835 million in capital. Cumulative investment has reached $6.4 billion, pointing to steady interest from both agricultural operators and energy developers.

At the farm level, biogas systems are reframing waste management economics. Organic waste streams—primarily manure but also food waste and wastewater—are being processed into usable outputs such as electricity, heat, renewable natural gas (RNG), and nutrient-rich fertilizer. Current infrastructure processes an estimated 25 billion gallons of manure annually, generating enough energy to supply around 800,000 homes.

This combination of emissions reduction and revenue generation is central to adoption. Methane capture helps address regulatory and sustainability pressures, while energy production creates an additional income stream tied to evolving energy markets.

Shift Toward RNG Signals Market Integration

The way biogas is used is also changing. In 2020, most systems were designed to produce electricity for on-site consumption. Today, roughly two-thirds are focused on producing renewable natural gas for pipeline injection or transportation fuel.

This transition reflects stronger market alignment. RNG can integrate into existing gas infrastructure and is increasingly used in sectors where electrification remains challenging, including heavy transport and industrial applications. As a result, projects are becoming less localized and more connected to regional and national energy markets.

Adoption remains concentrated within specific segments of agriculture. Dairy operations account for the majority of systems, representing about 79% of installations, while hog farms make up roughly 19%. Other farm types, including poultry and crop operations, contribute a smaller share. Geographically, development is clustered in states with supportive policies and strong agricultural bases, such as California, Wisconsin, New York, and North Carolina.

Despite recent growth, overall market penetration is still limited. Thousands of farms have the technical potential to deploy biogas systems but have not yet done so. Nearly 3,000 dairy farms are considered viable candidates, while adoption in the hog sector remains below 2% of eligible operations.

Barriers persist, particularly around upfront capital requirements, project complexity, and inconsistent regulatory frameworks. However, improving project economics and rising demand for low-carbon fuels are beginning to offset these constraints.

If adoption expands more broadly, the available resource base is significant. Farm-based biogas could generate enough additional energy to power an estimated 7.7 million homes, positioning it as a practical contributor to both domestic energy supply and emissions reduction targets.

text:
A federal district court on Wednesday ruled that Alabama Power may continue to charge an additional fee to households with rooftop solar panels.

U.S. District Court Judge Annemarie Carney Axon granted a motion filed by both Alabama Public Service Commission and Alabama Power that sought a summary judgement dismissing a lawsuit filed by plaintiffs to rescind the fee, known as a capacity charge, from their bills. Axon did not provide an opinion with the order.

Plaintiffs said in a statement Friday that they were disappointed with the ruling.

“I am frustrated that Alabama Power solar customers like me have to pay an extra monthly fee in order to reduce our power bills,” said Mark Johnston, an Episcopal priest and retired executive director of Camp McDowell.

He added that “I want lower electricity bills and a better environment for my children and grandchildren.”

Christina Tidwell, a senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, which represented the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in the statement that it was “a disappointing day for Alabama Power customers who want to use solar energy to get relief from some of the highest electricity bills in the nation.”

“Not only are we missing out on the bill savings that could be realized through installing rooftop solar, but we’re also missing out on opportunities for job creation and economic development,” the statement said.

Alabama Power said in a statement Friday that “customers who rely on the grid must help pay for the grid.”

“We are pleased the court agreed with the Public Service Commission’s determination that customers who choose to use Alabama Power for backup service should pay their share of costs to maintain the grid,” the statement said.

The company said it supports customers who want to install rooftop solar, but said those who want to connect with Alabama Power “must pay their share of grid costs so other customers are not unfairly burdened.”

The Alabama Public Service Commission in 2012 authorized Alabama Power to charge $5 for kilowatts of power that customers generate from their solar panels. The charge increased to $5.41 in September 2020. For a site with a 5kW solar array, that would cost an additional $25 per month or $300 annually. That amounts to about $9,000 in costs over the 30-year lifespan of a solar system.

That additional cost reduces the return for households and businesses that make installing solar panels to make the investment worthwhile.

Critics argue the additional fee reduces the incentives for people to install solar panels on their properties.

According to the Solar Energies Industry Association, Alabama at the end of last year had 966 mW of solar power installed in the state, accounting for less than 1% of total energy production. By comparison, South Carolina, demographically similar to Alabama, had 3,061 mW of solar power, generating about 3.8% of energy in that state. Mississippi, with about 57% of Alabama’s population, had 2,052 mW installed, about 3.7% of generation there.

title: EPA Announces $610 Million Loan to Provide a Reliable Source of Drinking Water to ...
description:

“No American should worry about the reliability of their drinking water,” said EPA Assistant Administrator for Water Jess Kramer.
The Water Commission member communities currently rely on a declining groundwater aquifer as their primary source of drinking water.

text:
March 27, 2026

WASHINGTON – U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced a $610 million Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (WIFIA) loan to the Grand Prairie Water Commission, which serves six communities in northeastern Illinois. This loan will transition almost 300,000 residents to Lake Michigan—a more reliable source of drinking water—from a declining groundwater aquifer.

“No American should worry about the reliability of their drinking water,” said EPA Assistant Administrator for Water Jess Kramer. “We are pleased that Grand Prairie Water Commission will use this investment to ensure its water customers have a stable and reliable source of drinking water for current and future generations.”

The Grand Prairie Water Commission is made up of six member communities including the Cities of Crest Hill and Joliet and the Villages of Channahon, Minooka, Shorewood, and Romeoville. The Water Commission member communities currently rely on a declining groundwater aquifer as their primary source of drinking water. EPA’s WIFIA financing will support the Commission’s Alternative Water Source Program. With this loan, the commission will construct a 62-mile regional water transmission network and upgrade other water infrastructure and systems. This project will enable these communities to transition from their primary source, a declining groundwater aquifer, to Lake Michigan’s reliable, high-quality source water. Establishing this alternative water source will ensure the commission can meet the drinking water needs of current and future customers.

“We thank the USEPA for making this critical funding assistance available and helping to keep the program affordable for our member communities,” said Shorewood Mayor CC DeBold, GPWC Board of Commissioners Chair. “Fueled by this investment, we look forward to continuing our progress toward delivery of a new, reliable water source by 2030.”

EPA’s WIFIA program will provide the commission flexibility through the ability to customize repayment schedules and defer principal payments for several years after substantial completion of construction, saving the commission nearly $300 million over the life of the loan.

EPA’s WIFIA program provides a powerful financial tool that can significantly accelerate investments in water infrastructure to protect human health and the environment while saving communities millions of dollars. Since issuing its first loan in 2018, EPA’s WIFIA program has announced $23 billion in financing water infrastructure projects that are strengthening drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater infrastructure while creating over 168,000 jobs. Through its flexible financing features and competitive interest rates, WIFIA helps communities save money, and accelerate water infrastructure investments.

WIFIA funding is available to support additional water infrastructure projects, including up to $6.5 billion available to water systems and another $550 million available to State infrastructure financing authorities. EPA is currently accepting letters of interest.

Learn more about EPA’s WIFIA program and water infrastructure investments, including how to submit a letter of interest.

text:
Meta’s agreement with New Orleans–based Entergy, announced March 27, is to build and finance seven new power plants in Louisiana. That comes on top of plans approved last year to build three gas power plants for the sprawling AI hub. The 10 power plants with 7.5 gigawatts of capacity would represent a more than 30% increase to Louisiana’s entire grid capacity, not even counting up to 2.5 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity, including battery storage, that Meta also agreed to help fund.

Meta initially announced plans for a $10 billion investment in December 2024 for a 2,250-acre data center campus in northeastern Louisiana in rural Richland Parish. But Meta recently, and quietly, acquired an additional 1,400 acres, as Fortune reported in February. In October 2025, Meta entered a joint venture with funds managed by Blue Owl Capital to finance, build, and operate the Hyperion campus with up to $27 billion in total development costs, seemingly ensuring the mega-campus will serve as a long-term, multiphase AI hub.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Hyperion would cover a “significant part of the footprint of Manhattan.”

“Our Richland Parish data center serves as a symbol of the ambition and scale of next-generation AI infrastructure,” said Rachel Peterson, Meta vice president for data centers, in a statement. “We are building foundations for the future of AI innovation right here in the United States. We’ve been working closely with Entergy since early on-site planning to ensure our power needs are met and, importantly, so that Entergy’s other consumers aren’t paying our costs.”

The Louisiana Public Service Commission will still need to approve the projects. The previous three power plants received regulatory authorization last year.

Entergy’s stock jumped 7% on March 27, lifting its market cap to a new record high of about $50 billion. The stock has risen almost 125% in two years.

Entergy is emphasizing that Meta is paying for the projects, rather than shifting the costs to other ratepayers. Entergy argues that the deals will save Louisiana taxpayers billions of dollars over several years.

The 10 power plants are estimated to cost nearly $11 billion. Critics contend ratepayers could be stuck with the bill after 15 years, which is the length of the contractual terms, if Meta no longer requires so much power after that span.

“This agreement reflects what’s possible when strong partners align around long-term growth and value,” said Phillip May, president and CEO of Entergy Louisiana, in a statement. “Working with our customers, regulators, and state leaders, we are making targeted investments that strengthen reliability, support economic development, and deliver meaningful benefits to customers—all while keeping energy rates affordable.”

text:
SASKATOON — Canada’s canola sector is pumped about a long-awaited biofuel policy decision in the United States.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has announced its final Renewable Volume Obligation (RVO) blending rule for biomass-based diesel.

The EPA set the blending mandate for biodiesel and renewable diesel to 5.4 billion gallons in 2026 and 5.5 billion gallons in 2027.

Read Also

Caution keeps pastureland values in check

Pastureland values increased about five percent last year in Western Canada. Meanwhile, cropland jumped 10 per cent.

That is a 61 to 64 per cent increase over the 2025 level of 3.35 billion gallons.

“We’re very pleased to see those updates, and Canadian canola can make a meaningful contribution there,” said Canola Council of Canada president Chris Davison.

Why it Matters: The U.S. is the biggest buyer of Canadian canola oil.

He has not yet seen the EPA’s official regulatory text, but based on the agency’s announcement, there does not appear to be anything preventing Canadian canola oil from helping to meet the feedstock demand for the new RVOs.

“Canola is a modest but important feedstock in U.S. biomass-based diesel production,” said Davis.

The new RVOs should create an “appreciable opportunity” for Canada’s canola crushers who have greatly increased production capacity in recent years.

U.S. oilseed groups were thrilled with the EPA’s announcement.

The American Soybean Association said soybean farmers needed a win to boost domestic markets, and U.S. president Donald Trump’s administration delivered “in a big way.”

“The 2026-27 RVOs will increase soybean oil use, boost U.S. soybean processing and grow domestic biofuel markets for our crop,” ASA president Scott Metzger stated in a press release.

The final rule also reallocates 70 per cent of retroactive small refinery exemption volumes dating back to 2016 back into the blending pool to support additional biofuel production and soybean demand.

The only letdown for U.S. soybean growers was that they did not get their wish for the rule to prioritize domestically sourced biofuel feedstocks in 2026 and 2027.

However, the EPA announced that it will reduce credit generation for imported biofuels and biofuel feedstocks by half, beginning in 2028.

If the EPA lives up to that promise, it would serve as a significant additional economic driver for the U.S. soybean sector, according to the association.

Davison is not sure what the EPA means by imported biofuel and feedstocks. At one point, the agency was considering a proposal to create a ring fence covering all of North America, and anything outside that zone would be considered imported.

He needs to see the details of the regulation to figure out what the EPA is considering for 2028.

The U.S. biofuel industry accounts for more than half of all U.S. domestic soybean oil consumption.

Clean Fuels Alliance America noted that biodiesel and renewable diesel facilities were forced to shut down or run far below previous year levels in 2025 due to market uncertainty.

U.S. biodiesel production declined by one-third compared to 2024 levels.

“The robust biomass-based diesel volumes set in this rule support America’s farmers and consumers,” Kurt Kovarik, Clean Fuel’s vice-president of federal affairs, stated in a press release.

Demand from the biodiesel and renewable diesel sector accounts for 10 per cent of the value of every bushel of U.S. grown soybeans.

The National Oilseed Processors Association called it a “landmark rule” that provides certainty and confidence for American farmers and processors.

“The historic volumes for biomass-based diesel, the 70 per cent reallocation of waived gallons, and the commitment to account for SREs (small refinery exemptions) on a go-forward basis, restores program integrity and puts the RFS (renewable fuel standard) back on a growth trajectory,” association president Devin Mogler said in a press release.

text:
Data centers: lead-acid strength and lithium trials

O’Connell highlighted EnerSys’ historical position in data centers, stating the company holds roughly 55% U.S. market share in lead-acid batteries used for data center power. He said EnerSys’ installed base and relationships with UPS original equipment manufacturers—citing Vertiv, Schneider, and Eaton—as well as direct engagement with hyperscalers, put it in what he called “high trust environments” where availability and service readiness are critical.

→ Is 2026 the Year of Space Stocks? 2 Stocks to Watch

While the company expects its lead-acid data center business to grow about 20% this year, O’Connell characterized lithium as the larger growth vector, noting lithium accounts for roughly 60% to 70% of greenfield AI-related data centers. He said EnerSys launched its first customer trials of a lithium data center battery offering “this month,” with efforts focused on product validation, communications with UPS systems, and performance in the operating environment.

On timing, O’Connell said EnerSys is “level setting” expectations that the sales lift from lithium in data centers is likely to begin showing up in fiscal 2028 (the company operates on an April-to-March fiscal year). He added that batteries are often ordered late in data center build cycles, even when upstream components such as transformers carry multi-year lead times.

800-volt DC transition and power quality opportunity

→ GE Vernova: AI's Thirst for Power Creates a New Class of Winner

Executives also addressed the industry’s transition toward 800-volt DC architectures. O’Connell said EnerSys has long provided DC systems via batteries, with the main change being a move from traditional 480-volt designs to 800-volt designs to improve efficiency and reduce copper requirements. He said the shift should be a “lift in volume” for EnerSys because it would require more cells per system.

Separately, O’Connell discussed power quality needs in AI environments, describing battery technology as a near-term tool for managing rapid swings in load. He said using batteries for power quality can accelerate battery wear, which could increase replacement demand over time. He also pointed to an opportunity for rapidly deployable, smaller-scale power systems at the edge—an area where he said EnerSys has experience through its telecommunications, cable, and broadband businesses.

South Carolina lithium plant: pivot toward defense domestication

EnerSys addressed its planned lithium facility in South Carolina, describing a strategic shift in how the project is framed. O’Connell said the factory was initially conceived during the Biden administration when incentives were oriented toward EV supply chains, but that subsequent policy emphasis on “foreign entity of concern” (FEOC) rules and changes to EV credits altered the original premise. He said EnerSys has since pivoted discussions toward supporting U.S. government goals to domesticize battery supply for the military, citing the risk of reliance on China for soldier power programs.

O’Connell called the company’s statements “aspirational” until final government “definitization,” but said discussions have been positive. He described a government objective to consolidate numerous soldier power-related battery programs into fewer programs and suggested EnerSys could support that effort. He also said a defense-focused strategy could be less exposed to open-market pricing dynamics because sales would be tied to programs rather than competing against commercial pack price declines.

Funk said the company has received a $200 million Department of Energy grant (a grant, not a loan) that it is seeking to reaffirm, noting it is a cost-share program and could be adjusted based on scope changes. She also cited about $200 million of South Carolina incentives, which she characterized as longer-term. Both executives said more detailed updated financials would be provided when plans are communicated, and at an investor day on June 11 at the New York Stock Exchange.

Capital allocation: internal investment, acquisitions, buybacks, and 45X benefits

Funk outlined EnerSys’ capital allocation priorities, starting with internal investment. She said ongoing capital expenditures for the existing lead-acid footprint are expected to be about $75 million to $100 million before considering the new lithium plant, and noted that this is below depreciation.

On external growth, Funk said EnerSys has completed more than 36 acquisitions since 2004 and continues to favor deals in the $100 million to $300 million range that are in growth markets and margin accretive, rather than turnarounds or early-stage startups. She also said the board has authorized a $1 billion share repurchase program, and that the company has been buying back stock “pretty aggressively.”

Funk also discussed EnerSys’ 45X benefits, saying the company receives about $40 million per quarter, treated as a reduction in cost of sales and not subject to tax. She said the credit currently offsets federal income tax liability and referenced an expected $120 million refund that was due “this month,” adding that any delay would be received with interest. Funk linked the incentive to decisions to invest in U.S. capacity, including moving production from Monterrey to Kentucky and announcing the closure of a Tijuana plant with production moving largely to Missouri.

O’Connell said his “Energize” program—focused on optimizing the core business, tightening the operating model through centers of excellence, and accelerating growth—has progressed ahead of expectations, pointing to cost reductions, operating effectiveness, and faster execution on customer-driven redesign work. He reiterated that EnerSys competes in different markets than large EV-focused battery players, emphasizing that the company’s value add extends beyond the cell through integration, communications, regulatory requirements, and service.

About Enersys (NYSE:ENS)

Enersys, headquartered in Reading, Pennsylvania, is a global leader in stored energy solutions, specializing in manufacturing and distributing industrial batteries, battery chargers, power equipment, and related accessories. The company serves a diverse range of end markets, including telecommunications, data centers, medical, aerospace, defense, electric vehicle motive power, and utility outcomes. Its products are engineered to deliver critical reserve power and motive power applications across key infrastructure and industrial sectors.

The company's product portfolio encompasses lead-acid batteries, lithium-ion energy storage systems, chargers, inverters, power management software, and a broad array of battery accessories.
